lead: Speech recognition does not need every sample of the waveform. It needs a short vector every 10 ms that says what the vocal tract is doing. The MFCC pipeline turns each frame into 13 cepstral coefficients: pre-emphasis, framing, windowing, DFT, a mel filterbank, log, and DCT. For storage or transmission, speech coding compresses the waveform itself: PCM at 64 kbps, LPC vocoders near 2.4 kbps, and hybrid CELP coders such as GSM, G.729 and Opus. Features feed recognisers; coders save bits.
prereq: You need: 7.3 for the DFT and windows, and 7.4 for the mel scale and why bands are spaced that way.

blocks.text: A feature vector is a small set of numbers that summarises one frame of speech. The most common set is the mel-frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC); some syllabi call it the mel-frequency cepstral coefficient. The aim is to keep the shape of the vocal-tract spectrum and throw away pitch detail and channel effects.

items: Pre-emphasis: replace each sample by y[n] = x[n] − 0.97x[n−1]. This lifts the high frequencies, which speech loses naturally.
Frame the signal into 25 ms windows with a 10 ms hop. At 16 kHz, one frame holds 400 samples and the hop is 160 samples.
Multiply each frame by a window, usually Hamming, so the edges taper to zero and the DFT does not see a sudden cut.
Compute a 512-point DFT of the windowed frame. Keep the magnitude spectrum.
Pass the spectrum through a mel filterbank: 26 triangular filters spaced by the mel scale, dense at low frequencies.
Take the log of each filter energy. The log turns multiplication by a channel gain into addition.
Apply the DCT. The low-order cepstral coefficients describe the smooth spectral envelope.
Keep c1 to c12 or c1 to c13. c0 carries frame energy. The rest are discarded.

blocks.where: x[n] is the input sample at time index n; y[n] is the pre-emphasised sample; 0.97 is a typical pre-emphasis coefficient.

sections.h3: Motion, channel and other feature sets

blocks.text: A single MFCC frame is a snapshot. Speech is motion, so we add deltas and delta-deltas. A delta is the slope of a coefficient over nearby frames; a delta-delta is the slope of the delta. With 13 MFCCs, 13 deltas and 13 delta-deltas, the vector has 39 dimensions. At 100 frames per second this gives 3900 feature numbers per second.

blocks.where: c<sub>t</sub> is the coefficient vector at frame t; μ is the mean vector over the utterance; ĉ<sub>t</sub> is the cepstral-mean-normalised vector. This removes a fixed channel effect such as a microphone colour.

items: LPC (linear predictive coding) models each sample as a weighted sum of past samples. A common order rule is order ≈ f<sub>s</sub>(kHz) + 2, so 10 at 8 kHz and 18 at 16 kHz.
PLP (perceptual linear prediction) uses auditory smoothing before LPC; it is an alternative front end to MFCC.
CMN is cepstral mean normalisation. It is cheap and improves robustness to a fixed channel.

sections.h3: Speech coding: waveform, source and hybrid

blocks.text: Speech coding reduces the bit rate needed to send or store speech. Bit rate is bits per second, not samples per second. A waveform coder sends samples or a close approximation. PCM at 8 kHz sampling and 8 bits per sample gives 8000 × 8 = 64 kbps. Companding (μ-law or A-law) first compresses the amplitude scale, so quiet sounds get more codes than loud ones; this improves perceived quality at the same bit count.

A source coder sends parameters of the speech model, not the waveform. An LPC vocoder at about 2.4 kbps is intelligible but sounds robotic. A hybrid coder combines a waveform code with a source model; the CELP family is the main example. Quality is scored by MOS, the mean opinion score, on a scale from 1 (bad) to 5 (excellent). A coder is judged by both MOS and bit rate.

figure.caption: The MFCC chain for one 25 ms frame: 400 samples with a 160-sample hop (100 frames/s) become 13 cepstral coefficients; adding deltas and delta-deltas gives 39 dimensions, or 3900 feature values per second.

spec.title: MFCC computation for one frame
spec.aria: A vertical chain of blocks from pre-emphasis through framing, windowing, 512-point DFT, 26-triangle mel filterbank, log, and DCT, ending with 13 MFCCs plus deltas and delta-deltas for 39 dimensions and 3900 feature values per second.

examples.question: At 16 kHz, speech is framed into 25 ms frames with a 10 ms hop. Find the frame length in samples, the hop in samples, frames per second, the feature dimension for 13 MFCCs plus 13 deltas plus 13 delta-deltas, feature numbers per second, and the ratio of raw samples to feature numbers. For 8 kHz, 8-bit PCM find the bit rate, find the saving factor against G.729 at 8 kbps, and find the LPC order at 16 kHz.
steps: Frame length N = 25 ms × 16 samples/ms = 400 samples. Equivalently N = 0.025 s × 16000 samples/s = 400 samples.
Frames per second F = 1 / 0.010 s = 100 frames/s.
Feature numbers per second R = 100 frames/s × 39 = 3900 feature numbers/s.
Raw samples per second S = 16000 samples/s. Ratio S/R = 16000 / 3900 = 4.102564102564102, about 4.10 raw samples per feature number.
PCM bit rate = 8000 samples/s × 8 bits/sample = 64000 bits/s = 64 kbps.
Saving against G.729 = 64 kbps / 8 kbps = 8. G.729 uses 8 times fewer bits per second.
examples.answer: The 16 kHz example has 400-sample frames, 160-sample hops, 100 frames/s, 39-dimensional vectors, 3900 feature values/s, and a 4.10:1 reduction from raw samples; 8 kHz 8-bit PCM is 64 kbps, G.729 saves 8 times, and the LPC order is 18.
examples.check:
fs = 16000
frame_ms = 25
hop_ms = 10
mfcc = 13
delta_sets = 3
N = frame_ms / 1000 * fs
H = hop_ms / 1000 * fs
F = 1000 / hop_ms
D = mfcc * delta_sets
R = F * D
ratio = fs / R
Bpcm = 8000 * 8 / 1000
saving = Bpcm / 8
lpc16 = 16 + 2
print(int(N))
print(int(H))
print(int(F))
print(D)
print(int(R))
print(fs)
print(ratio)
print(int(Bpcm))
print(int(saving))
print(lpc16)

traps: Wrong order: pre-emphasis comes before framing, and the log comes after the mel filterbank but before the DCT.
The DCT output is truncated, not kept whole. Keeping all coefficients keeps pitch detail and channel colour; the recogniser usually wants c1 to c12 or c13.
Bit rate is not sample rate. A coder can keep 8 kHz sampling at 8 kbps because it sends parameters, not one code per sample.
c0 is not a normal cepstral shape coefficient; it carries frame energy. Many systems drop it or treat it separately.
Do not confuse the 25 ms frame length with the 10 ms hop. The hop controls how many frames per second; the frame length controls the DFT window.

quiz.q: What does MFCC stand for, and what is the final output before deltas?
quiz.a: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient. The final output is a short vector of cepstral coefficients, usually c1 to c12 or c1 to c13, with c0 carrying energy.

quiz.q: Why is the log taken after the mel filterbank and before the DCT?
quiz.a: The log turns a channel gain multiplying each filter energy into an additive constant. The DCT then separates the smooth spectral envelope from the finer pitch detail.

quiz.q: At 8 kHz, use 20 ms frames, a 10 ms hop, and 12 MFCCs plus deltas plus delta-deltas. Find the frame length in samples, frames per second, feature dimension, and feature numbers per second.
Why does pre-emphasis come before framing in the MFCC pipeline?
quiz.a: Pre-emphasis is a sample-by-sample filter, so it must act on the continuous sample stream before the stream is cut into frames. Applying it after framing would leave frame-edge effects and would not match the standard spectral tilt correction.

quiz.q: What is the bit rate of 8 kHz sampling with 8 bits per sample PCM?
State one difference between a waveform coder and a source coder.
quiz.a: A waveform coder sends samples or a close approximation of the waveform. A source coder sends parameters of a speech model, such as LPC filter coefficients and pitch, not the waveform itself.

quiz.q: Using the rule order ≈ f<sub>s</sub>(kHz) + 2, what LPC order is used at 8 kHz and at 16 kHz?
Why can a hybrid CELP coder sound better than a plain LPC vocoder at a similar low bit rate?
quiz.a: A plain LPC vocoder sends only a slowly varying filter and pitch, so it loses excitation detail. CELP adds a codebook search for the excitation, so the decoder can match the short-term waveform better while still sending parameters at a low bit rate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems often learn features directly from the waveform, as wav2vec and other self-supervised models do, replacing hand-built MFCCs. Neural speech codecs trade bit rate against quality using networks. Search for 'wav2vec 2.0', 'neural audio codec' and 'Opus codec' to go further.
